newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish markets fall on S&P downgrading.
newsitem.headline: Turkish markets fall on S&P downgrading.

text.p: Turkish shares fell more than five percent in early trading on Monday and the central bank sold dollars to support the lira in reaction to Standard & Poors' (S&P) downgrading of Turkey's long-term foreign currency debt.
The market index later recovered slightly, down 3.82 percent on the day at 85,927.47, with brokers saying the downgrading had been widely anticipated.

Bankers said they expected market calm to be quickly restored, citing the central bank's large foreign currency reserves and financial institutions' memories of 1994 when market panic over a similar downgrading caused large losses.

"The market may wait for the government's economic performance after the downgrading and watch financial markets to settle down. It is too early to guess the stock market's trend," said Huseyin Istanbullu from Meksa securities.

On Friday S&P cut its ratings of Turkey's long-term foreign currency debt to "single B" from "single B-plus" while reaffirming its rating of "single-B" for short-term foreign currency debt. It said the downgrade reflected worsening fiscal and debt service pressures as the coalition government failed to show the will to implement reforms to tackle the growing budget deficit.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has focused on privatisation and pushing through measures such as property sales, leasing of power stations and issuing foreign currency bonds to cut Turkey's huge budget deficit and domestic debt.

Turkey's economy is struggling under 80 percent annual inflation and a budget deficit expected to widen to 1,300 trillion lira ($12.3 billion), or 10 percent of gross domestic product, by the end of 1996.

Analysts say only a significant acceleration of Turkey's stalled privatisation process would make Erbakan's revenue plans feasible, but S&P said significant income from privatisation was unlikely before late 1997 at the earliest.
The privatisation agency targets revenues of some $5 billion from 1997 sell-offs, though only some $3 billion has been raised since the programme began in 1986.
The government's 1997 draft budget foresees a zero deficit, also seen as unrealistic by many bankers.

A run on the lira in early 1994, after both S&P and another agency, Moody's, downgraded the country's credit rating, plunged the country into a financial crisis. Markets fell sharply and the currency was devalued twice. The lira lost 65 percent of its value that year.
"The same factors as today sparked a crisis in 1994 after the markets panicked terribly," said a private banker in Istanbul. "They have now learned their lesson."

On Monday, the central bank, in a move to curb dollar demand spurred by the S&P news and a stronger dollar on world markets, intervened to sell dollars after the lira weakened to 105,400 to the dollar from Friday's 104,160 close. It firmed to 105,330 at noon.
"The central bank's strong foreign currency reserves will prevent the dollar from rising sharply," said Bora Cilek, assistant general manager at Midland Bank.
Yields on the bond market rose by between two and three points across the board amid nervousness following the S&P news.
"The bond market was also unnerved by the S&P decision which sparked selling and caused yields to rise. The market has not yet set a direction," said a bond market trader.
